title: Lumps — possible explanations and care navigation
content: Adapted project summary of NHS Website Content: most lumps are harmless, but a chat cannot identify a lump or rule out a serious cause. Examples of possible patterns include a soft squashy lump that moves, which can represent a lipoma; a smooth lump under the skin, which can represent a skin cyst; a swollen painful lump with fever, which can represent a skin abscess; and a swelling in the neck, armpit, or groin, which can represent a swollen gland. A painless lump that enlarges and later becomes painful is one pattern that needs assessment for a less common serious cause. These are examples, not diagnostic rules. Arrange an in-person review if a lump grows, is painful, red or hot, feels hard and does not move, returns after removal, is in the breast or testicle, or lasts more than two weeks. Note location, duration, size, growth, pain, warmth, mobility, drainage, fever, night sweats, weight loss, and effects on swallowing or breathing. An examination may be followed by ultrasound or biopsy when the cause is unclear. title: Coughing up blood — possible causes and urgent care navigation
content: Adapted project summary of NHS Website Content: coughing up blood has many possible causes and should be checked promptly. Examples include irritation after a long-lasting or severe cough; a lung or airway infection such as bronchitis, pneumonia, or tuberculosis; and bronchiectasis, in which widened airways can produce more mucus. Less common but important possibilities include a blood clot in the lung or lung cancer. These are examples, not a diagnosis. Seek urgent same-day medical assessment even for small spots, flecks, or streaks of blood in phlegm. Call local emergency services for more than a few spots or streaks, or when coughing blood occurs with difficulty breathing, a very fast heartbeat, or chest or upper-back pain. Track the amount, frequency, duration, whether blood is mixed with mucus, fever, breathlessness, pain, and medicines including blood thinners. title: Pregnancy nutrition — balanced food examples
content: Project-authored summary of FDA pregnancy nutrition guidance: a balanced pregnancy diet can include varied vegetables; whole fruits; low-fat dairy such as milk, yogurt, and cheese or fortified soy beverages; protein foods such as seafood, lean meat, poultry, eggs, beans, peas, nuts, seeds, and soy; oils; and grains, with at least half from whole grains. Concrete whole-grain examples include oats, barley, brown rice, bulgur, millet, quinoa, whole-wheat bread, whole-wheat chapati, and whole-grain cereals or crackers. Foods fortified with folic acid can include enriched bread, pasta, rice, breakfast cereals, and products made with fortified corn masa flour. Practical examples assembled from those foods include oatmeal with fruit and yogurt; brown rice with vegetables and beans or lean poultry; or whole-wheat bread with egg plus fruit. These are general examples, not a personalized meal plan. Pregnancy food choices also need to account for allergies, diabetes or other conditions, nausea, cultural preferences, and guidance from the person's prenatal clinician.

title: Iron-rich foods and food-pairing examples
publisher: National Institutes of Health Office of Dietary Supplements
content: Project-authored summary of the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements consumer fact sheet: examples of foods that provide iron include lean meat, seafood, poultry, iron-fortified breakfast cereals and breads, white beans, lentils, spinach, kidney beans, peas, nuts, and some dried fruits such as raisins. The body absorbs iron from plant sources better when they are eaten with meat, poultry, seafood, or vitamin C foods such as citrus fruit, strawberries, sweet peppers, tomatoes, and broccoli. Practical food-pairing examples assembled from those foods include lentils with tomatoes or sweet peppers; iron-fortified cereal with strawberries; spinach and white beans with broccoli; or lean poultry with peas. These are food examples, not a diagnosis of deficiency, a personalized diet, or a supplement recommendation. Iron supplements can be harmful in excess and should not be started or dosed from a chat response.

title: Traditional Chinese medicine — evidence and safety summary
publisher: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health
license: U.S. government public domain unless marked
content: Project-authored summary based on NCCIH: evidence varies across traditional Chinese medicine practices. Some research supports selected uses of acupuncture or tai chi, while studies of Chinese herbal products have mixed results. Safety problems reported for some products include undeclared ingredients, substitution, contamination, heavy metals, pesticides, and organ toxicity. Acupuncture should be delivered by a properly qualified practitioner using appropriate sterile technique.

title: Herb–medicine interactions — clinical caution summary
publisher: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health
license: U.S. government public domain unless marked
content: Project-authored summary based on NCCIH: herbal products can have pharmacologic effects, direct toxicities, contaminants, and interactions with prescription or over-the-counter medicines. Evidence for many suspected interactions remains limited or indirect, so uncertainty should be stated. Extra caution is warranted with medicines that have a narrow therapeutic index, anticoagulants, chemotherapy, transplant medicines, digoxin, and around surgery, pregnancy, or liver and kidney disease. A pharmacist or doctor should review the exact product and medication list.

title: Evidence-based traditional and integrative medicine policy
content: Project-authored policy summary: the WHO Traditional Medicine Strategy 2025–2034 emphasizes strengthening the evidence base, safety, effectiveness, appropriate regulation, qualified practice, and responsible integration into health systems. Inclusion of a traditional practice or classification is not proof that a specific intervention is effective. Patient-facing answers should distinguish cultural or traditional frameworks from evidence about benefits and harms.

title: Singapore Chinese proprietary medicine safeguards
content: Project-authored regulatory summary based on HSA: Chinese proprietary medicines sold in Singapore are subject to product-listing and dealer requirements, ingredient restrictions, contaminant limits, and labelling rules. The required sale statement advises consumer discretion. Consumers should use reputable sources, check current HSA information, and consult a registered TCM practitioner plus a pharmacist or doctor when medicines, pregnancy, surgery, allergies, or chronic disease could change risk.

title: Ankle pain — injury and care-navigation summary
content: Project-authored summary based on MedlinePlus: ankle pain after a twist may reflect a sprain, but fractures and injuries to tendons, cartilage, or nerves can cause similar symptoms. Limit weight on the ankle, elevate it, and use wrapped ice for short periods while arranging assessment when needed. Hospital assessment is appropriate for severe pain even without bearing weight, suspected fracture or deformity, inability to bear weight or move the ankle, a pop followed by immediate pain, or significant swelling. Contact a clinician if swelling does not improve in two to three days, infection signs develop, or pain persists.

title: Cough — duration and care-navigation summary
content: Project-authored summary based on MedlinePlus: coughing is a protective reflex. Acute coughs begin suddenly and usually last no more than two to three weeks, while longer coughs are considered chronic and have a broader range of possible causes, including asthma, allergies, chronic lung disease, reflux, smoking, throat disorders, and some medicines. Fluids may help ease a cough. Cough medicines require age-appropriate caution, and children under four should not receive cough medicine. Blood in coughed-up material belongs to the separate urgent hemoptysis pathway.

title: Chest pain — urgent care-navigation summary
content: Project-authored summary based on MedlinePlus: chest discomfort has many possible causes involving the heart, lungs, digestive tract, muscles, ribs, tendons, or nerves, and some causes are life-threatening. Heart-related pain may feel like tightness, heavy pressure, squeezing, or crushing and may spread to an arm, shoulder, jaw, or back. A chat cannot determine the cause. New, unexplained, severe, or pressure-like chest pain—especially with breathing difficulty, sweating, nausea, faintness, or spreading pain—requires emergency assessment rather than home diagnosis.

title: Abdominal pain — red flags and care-navigation summary
content: Project-authored summary based on MedlinePlus: pain intensity alone does not reliably show whether abdominal pain is serious. Immediate medical help is advised for sudden sharp abdominal pain, pain with chest, neck, or shoulder pain, vomiting blood or blood in stool, a stiff hard tender abdomen, or inability to pass stool with vomiting. Persistent or worsening pain and pain with other symptoms need clinician review. Location, onset, pattern, vomiting, bowel changes, urinary symptoms, fever, pregnancy possibility, and recent injury are useful details for assessment.

title: Headache — red flags and care-navigation summary
content: Project-authored summary based on MedlinePlus: headaches have many causes and most are not emergencies, but some warn of a serious disorder. Sudden severe headache, headache after a blow to the head, or headache with a stiff neck, fever, confusion, loss of consciousness, or eye or ear pain needs prompt medical help. A useful description includes how suddenly it began, location, severity, prior headache pattern, injury, fever, neck stiffness, vision or neurologic changes, medicines, and pregnancy status.

title: Fever — general information and care-navigation summary
content: Project-authored summary based on MedlinePlus: fever is a higher-than-normal body temperature and is usually a sign of illness or infection rather than a diagnosis itself. Other causes include medicines, heat illness, autoimmune disease, cancer, and some childhood vaccines. Fluids can help reduce dehydration risk. Age, measured temperature, measurement method, duration, immune status, pregnancy, recent travel or exposure, medicines, and accompanying symptoms determine how urgently a fever should be assessed. Children with fever should not receive aspirin.

title: Anaphylaxis — emergency-navigation summary
content: Project-authored summary based on MedlinePlus: anaphylaxis is a serious allergic reaction that can begin quickly and become life-threatening. Warning features can involve throat or tongue swelling, trouble swallowing, shortness of breath, wheezing, chest tightness, weak pulse, fainting, shock, widespread hives, vomiting, diarrhea, or cramps. Call local emergency services for a serious allergic reaction. If the person has an epinephrine auto-injector available for this purpose, use it right away according to their emergency plan while help is being summoned.
